- `readonly duration: number;`

  Seconds (the clip's, 0 for none).

- `readonly start: number;`
- `readonly frames: number;`

### BakedSkinnedAnimations

*class*

ENGINE EXTENSION (since API\_MINOR 43): `bakeSkinnedAnimations`'s result.

```ts
export class BakedSkinnedAnimations { … }
```

- `readonly isBakedSkinnedAnimations: true;`

- `readonly texture: DataTexture;`

  The bone matrices (the layout above): an InstancedSkinnedMesh binds it; a custom material may read it too (`textureLoad`).

- `readonly clips: readonly BakedSkinnedClip[];`
- `readonly bones: number;`

- `readonly frames: number;`

  All the clips' frames together.

- `readonly fps: number;`

- `readonly boundingSphere: Sphere;`

  The sphere every baked pose's vertices lie in, in the mesh's own space (each joint's matrices applied to the geometry's sphere): InstancedSkinnedMesh culls by it.

- `clipIndex(clip: number | string | AnimationClip): number;`

  A clip's index by index, name or the AnimationClip baked; -1 for none.

- `frameAt(clip: number | string | AnimationClip, time: number): number;`

  Where `time` (seconds) of a clip lies among all the frames: its `start` plus the frames into it (a fraction between two). Times wrap as a LoopRepeat action's, the duration exactly being the last frame. A RangeError for a clip not baked.

- `readonly boneNames: readonly string[];`

  Since API\_MINOR 44 (INSTANCED\_BONE\_OVERRIDES\_MINOR): the baked skeleton's bone names by index (what `setBoneOverrideJoints` takes); empty for animations baked by an older game.

- `matrixTable(): Float32Array;`

  Since API\_MINOR 45 (BAKED\_MATRIX\_TABLES\_MINOR): the bone matrix table, a copy: frames × bones matrices of 12 numbers (the layout above without the header and the rows: frame after frame, clip after clip, bone after bone), what `fromMatrices` takes. A TypeError once the texture is disposed or its data released.

- ```ts
  static fromMatrices(
      matrices: Float32Array,
      options: {
        bones: number;
        clips: readonly {
          name?: string;
          frames: number;
          duration?: number;
          clip?: AnimationClip;
        }[];
        fps?: number;
        boundingSphere?: Sphere;
        geometry?: BufferGeometry;
        mesh?: SkinnedMesh;
      },
    ): BakedSkinnedAnimations;
  ```

  Since API\_MINOR 45 (BAKED\_MATRIX\_TABLES\_MINOR): baked animations from a bone matrix table the game holds (`matrixTable()`'s layout, say a bake kept from an earlier run, or matrices worked out by the game), without sampling clips on a SkinnedMesh. `clips` gives each clip's frames in order (and its name, its duration, default the AnimationClip's or (frames − 1) / fps, and the AnimationClip, made empty when left out); `fps` (default 30) is kept in the header. `boundingSphere` is the sphere every pose lies in (copied); without it one is made from `geometry` (or the mesh's) moved by every matrix, as the bake makes it, else it is empty (no culling). `mesh`, the SkinnedMesh the table was baked from (its skeleton of `bones` bones), keeps the skeleton for bone overrides and `boneNames`; without it `setBoneOverrideJoints` is a TypeError. The numbers are not checked one by one (a NaN draws nothing). A TypeError for a table that is not a Float32Array; a RangeError for `bones` outside 1–65,536, a clip's frames that are not a whole number of at least 1, a table of another length than frames × bones × 12 or past bakeSkinnedAnimations' limits.

- `dispose(): void;`

### bakeSkinnedAnimations

*function*

```ts
export function bakeSkinnedAnimations(
    mesh: SkinnedMesh,
    clips: readonly AnimationClip[],
    options?: { fps?: number; root?: Object3D },
  ): BakedSkinnedAnimations;
```

ENGINE EXTENSION (since API\_MINOR 43, INSTANCED\_SKINNING\_MINOR): samples each clip on `mesh` (a SkinnedMesh bound to its skeleton) with an AnimationMixer on `root` (default the mesh's topmost ancestor below a Scene, else the mesh) at `fps` (default 30) and keeps each frame's bone matrices in a texture. Each frame's matrices are what the SkinnedMesh's vertex stage would use posed by a mixer at that time (LoopOnce, clamped at the end). The pose of everything under `root` is put back. It runs in script once (each frame a mixer update and a skeleton walk: bake at load). Errors: a RangeError past the limits above, a TypeError for a mesh without a skeleton or a clip that is not an AnimationClip.

### InstancedSkinnedMesh

*class*

ENGINE EXTENSION (since API\_MINOR 43, SKIN\_ATTRIBUTES\_MINOR and INSTANCED\_SKINNING\_MINOR): an InstancedMesh with a skin. Its geometry's `skinIndex` and `skinWeight` reach custom materials' vertex hooks as `Vertex.skin_index` and `Vertex.skin_weight`. With `bakedAnimations` each instance is skinned where `setAnimationAt` put it, in every pass, built-in materials and hooks alike (a hook's `Vertex.position` and `normal` arrive skinned, as on a SkinnedMesh); without them the vertices are not moved. Its place in the animations is the instance's custom slot 3 (`instanceCustom` becomes 16 numbers an instance, `customSlots` 4; slots 0 to 2 stay the game's, and `setCustomAt(i, v, 3)` is a RangeError; hooks read slot 3 as `Vertex.instance3`: x the frame of the first clip, y the second's, z the second's weight, w 1; since API\_MINOR 44 w is 2 + the instance's index, its bone overrides' row). It culls by the animations' sphere. It has no levels of detail (`setLevels` with anything but `[]` is a TypeError). Its sync runs in script (InstancedMesh's native sync is for InstancedMesh's own). DIFFERENCES from a SkinnedMesh posed by a mixer: between baked frames the two around are blended linearly (a mixer slerps each bone: at 30 fps the poses differ by well under a pixel for most rigs), and a crossfade blends the two clips' final matrices linearly (a mixer blends each bone's transform, then walks the rig). Motion vectors take each instance's place the frame before from its kept instances, so a crowd's limbs leave no trail under temporal anti-aliasing.

```ts
export class InstancedSkinnedMesh extends InstancedMesh { … }
```

- ```ts
  constructor(
      geometry: BufferGeometry,
      material: Material,
      count: number,
      bakedAnimations?: BakedSkinnedAnimations | null,
    );
  ```

- `readonly isInstancedSkinnedMesh: true;`

- `bakedAnimations: BakedSkinnedAnimations | null;`

  The animations its instances play, or null (settable).

- ```ts
  setAnimationAt(
      index: number,
      clip: number | string | AnimationClip,
      time: number,
      clip2?: number | string | AnimationClip,
      time2?: number,
      weight?: number,
    ): this;
  ```

  Instance `index` at `time` seconds of `clip` (an index, a name or the AnimationClip baked), crossfading toward `time2` of `clip2` by `weight` (0 to 1; none with -1 or a weight of 0). Times wrap as `frameAt`'s. Sets `instanceCustom.needsUpdate`. A TypeError without animations, a RangeError for an instance or clip that is not there.

#### Bone overrides (since API\_MINOR 44, INSTANCED\_BONE\_OVERRIDES\_MINOR)

ENGINE EXTENSION: per-instance local rotations of a few joints on top of the shared clip (foot placement and foot locking on slopes, a head turned toward a target), applied after the clip's sample and before the bone hierarchy: a joint's descendants follow it, in every pass (colour, shadows, prepasses, motion vectors), built-in materials and hooks alike, on every backend.

```text
crowd.setBoneOverrideJoints(["thigh.L", "shin.L", "foot.L", "thigh.R", "shin.R", "foot.R"]);
const legs = new Float32Array(crowd.count * 6 * 4); // instance-major, joint, xyzw
// each frame: solve each robot's leg IK into `legs`, then
crowd.setBoneOverrides(legs);
```

A joint's local transform is its parent bone's world inverse times its own world, read from the baked pose where the instance stands (frames and crossfade blended as the vertex stage blends them; a bone without a parent bone is local to the mesh's own space). "replace" sets its rotation (three.js `bone.quaternion.copy(q)`), "multiply" turns the clip's by it (`bone.quaternion.multiply(q)`); its position and scale stay the clip's. Nested joints compose down the chain whatever order they are listed in. A quaternion of four zeros is no override (the clip's pose); others are normalized.

COST: the runtime turns each frame's quaternions into one 3×4 correction a joint an instance (about 0.25 ms of one CPU core a frame for 200 instances × 6 joints, none for instances without overrides), sent to the GPU as a texture of 48 bytes a correction (61 KB for 200 × 6; 1,536 texels a row) that the vertex stage reads only for bones under an overridden joint. `setBoneOverrides` charges 1 fuel unit a number (4 a quaternion), as instance custom data does. The texture rides with the instances (not the image budget), as instance buffers do. DIFFERENCES from posing a SkinnedMesh's bones: the corrected joint's matrix is the blended baked one turned rigidly, so between frames and mid-crossfade it carries the blend's slight shear as the clip's own pose does; the culling sphere stays the baked poses' (an override reaching far outside it may be culled early); motion vectors take this frame's corrections for the frame before. Copies and clones start without overrides.

- `readonly boneOverrideJoints: readonly number[];`

  The declared joints (baked skeleton bone indices), in the order the overrides' data takes them; empty before `setBoneOverrideJoints`.

- `readonly boneOverrideMode: "replace" | "multiply";`

  How an override takes its joint's rotation.

- ```ts
  setBoneOverrideJoints(
      joints: readonly (number | string)[] | null,
      mode?: "replace" | "multiply",
      options?: { root?: number | string | boolean | null },
    ): this;
  ```

  Declares 1 to 16 joints (bone indices or `boneNames`) whose local rotation each instance may override, every override cleared, and sets each instance's custom slot 3's w to 2 + its index (its row); `null` takes the overrides away (so do new `bakedAnimations`). A TypeError without baked animations (or ones baked below 1.44) or for a mode that is neither; a RangeError for an unknown or repeated joint, past 16 joints or past 522,752 overrides (capacity × joints).

- `setBoneOverrides(data: Float32Array | null, first?: number): this;`

  Writes overrides from instance `first` (default 0): for each instance in turn, for each declared joint in order, a quaternion's x, y, z, w (`data.length` a multiple of 4, at most (capacity − first) × joints × 4; zeros: none). `null` clears every override. The one call a frame for a whole crowd: the numbers are copied, so the array may be reused. A RangeError for numbers past the capacity, a length not whole quaternions or a NaN or infinite number (nothing written); a TypeError before `setBoneOverrideJoints` or for anything but a Float32Array.

- ```ts
  setBoneOverrideAt(
      index: number,
      joint: number | string,
      quaternion: Quaternion | null,
    ): this;
  ```

  One instance's override of one declared joint (its place in `boneOverrideJoints`, or its bone name); null for none.

- `clearBoneOverrides(): this;`

  Every instance's overrides cleared (the joints kept).

#### Root offsets (since API\_MINOR 45, INSTANCED\_ROOT\_OFFSETS\_MINOR)

ENGINE EXTENSION: a per-instance translation of a root joint beside the rotation overrides (a crouch, a stagger, a hip bob, root motion taken out of a clip), named by `setBoneOverrideJoints(joints, mode, { root })`: `true` for the baked skeleton's first bone without a parent bone, or a bone index or name; the joints may then be `[]`. Each instance's offset is added to that joint's local translation (in its parent bone's space; the mesh's own for a root bone) after the clip's sample and its rotation override, so everything below it follows, in every pass on every backend. A root that is not among the joints takes a correction slot of its own (the texture and the cost above count it as a joint). Offsets are cleared with the joints; `setBoneOverrides(null)` and `clearBoneOverrides` leave them.

- `readonly rootOffsetJoint: number;`

  The root joint (bone index) `setRootOffsets` moves; -1 without.

- `setRootOffsets(data: Float32Array | null, first?: number): this;`

  Writes root offsets from instance `first` (default 0): x, y, z an instance (`data.length` a multiple of 3, at most (capacity − first) × 3; zeros: none); `null` clears them. 1 fuel unit a number. A RangeError for numbers past the capacity, a length not whole vectors or a NaN or infinite number (nothing written); a TypeError without a root joint or for anything but a Float32Array.

- `setRootOffsetAt(index: number, offset: Vector3 | null): this;`

  One instance's root offset; null for none.

## Levels of detail generation (since API\_MINOR 40)

### SimplifyModifier

*class*

three.js r185's addon `SimplifyModifier` (examples/jsm/modifiers/SimplifyModifier.js), exported here as the engine has no addons path (since API\_MINOR 40; before it the constructor is a TypeError). `modify(geometry, count)` gives a new indexed geometry with `count` fewer vertices, counted as three.js counts them after merging vertices whose position, uv, normal, tangent and color agree within 1e-4 (`BufferGeometryUtils.mergeVertices`), and those attributes as Float32 attributes; morph targets, groups and other attributes go, as in three.js. A count of 0 (or NaN) removes none; a count that never counts down to 0 (negative, fractional, Infinity) as many as can go. DIFFERENCE: the engine chooses what goes by quadric error (half-edge collapse after Solstice's builder: every surviving vertex is an original one, UV seams and hard edges keep their sides' attributes, open borders never move, and a texture sliding counts as error) rather than three.js's Melax cost, so the triangles differ from three.js's for the same count. The same input gives the same output bits natively and in browsers.

```ts
export class SimplifyModifier { … }
```

- `constructor();`
- `modify(geometry: BufferGeometry, count: number): BufferGeometry;`

### GenerateLodsOptions

*interface*

ENGINE EXTENSION: `generateLods`'s options.

```ts
export interface GenerateLodsOptions { … }
```

- `levels?: number;`

  Levels made beyond the mesh's own: 1 to 16 (default 3; an InstancedMesh takes at most 7). Fewer come back where another level would not drop a twentieth of the triangles.

- `ratio?: number;`

  Each level's triangles as a fraction of the one before, above 0 and below 1 (default 0.5).

- `errorPx?: number;`

  The most pixels a level may be off where it shows (default 1).

- `thin?: boolean;`

  Thin a mesh of many (8 or more) separate small pieces, such as grass blades or leaves: each level keeps about `ratio` of the pieces (spread evenly by where they are, each level's among the last's) and enlarges the survivors, flat ones across first, tubes thicker, so the total area stays the same (default false). Pieces much wider than most, and the rest of the mesh, simplify as usual.

- `camera?: PerspectiveCamera;`

  The camera whose `fov` the distances are for (default a fov of 50, PerspectiveCamera's default).

- `screenHeight?: number;`

  The viewport height in pixels the distances are for (default 1080).

- `hysteresis?: number;`

  Each level's hysteresis, as `LOD.addLevel` takes it (default 0).

- `lockBorders?: boolean;`

  Since API\_MINOR 48 (`LOD_OPEN_BORDERS_MINOR`; older games' is not read): false lets open borders, and seams where three or more triangles meet, move along themselves, their movement counted as error, so a mesh of open pieces (leaf cards, open shells, sheets meeting at seams) simplifies past the floor its locked borders set, each piece down to one triangle (default true: they stay where they are). A crown of separate small pieces thins better with `thin`.

- `impostor?: boolean | { size?: number };`

  Since API\_MINOR 48 (`LOD_IMPOSTOR_MINOR`; older games' is not read): a last level of three crossed cards through the centre of the mesh's bounds (two upright at right angles and one level), textured with the mesh as seen straight at each, baked on the CPU into one atlas of `size`-texel square tiles (8 to 256, default 64), drawn alpha tested by a `MeshStandardMaterial` of its own (the level's `material`, its `shadowSide` `BackSide`: each upright card is a pair of triangles a side and the level card faces up, casting nothing onto them; its geometry's `userData.impostor` true; 10 triangles). A texel takes the nearest surface's colour: vertex colours times the material's `color`, times its `map` where that is a `DataTexture` of RGBA8 data (other maps are not read: the colour alone). Its `lodError` is the farthest the mesh lies from the cards (at least the level before's), so in a `LodBudget` it draws where that is within `errorPx`, or where the budget runs out. For foliage seen from afar; an InstancedMesh's impostor counts among its 7 levels.

### generateLods

*function*

```ts
export function generateLods(mesh: InstancedMesh, options?: GenerateLodsOptions): InstancedMesh;
```

ENGINE EXTENSION (since API\_MINOR 40; before it a TypeError): levels of detail from a mesh's simplified geometries, made by quadric half-edge collapse as `SimplifyModifier` makes them, every surviving vertex keeping all its own attributes (UV seams, normals, colors, tangents and skin weights exactly) and open borders kept. Each level has about `ratio` of the triangles of the one before and its error in world units (the farthest any source vertex lies from it, how far a texture slid or changed weights could move a vertex, how far thinning moved one; more than the level before's, a level no farther off replacing it so no two switch at one distance) in its geometry's `userData.lodError`. A level shows from the camera distance where that error spans `errorPx` pixels on a `screenHeight`-pixel viewport: `error × screenHeight / (2 tan(fov / 2) × errorPx)`.

For a Mesh: a three.js `LOD` taking the mesh's name and transform, level 0 a mesh of its own geometry and each further level one of a simplified geometry, all sharing its material and shadow flags (a SkinnedMesh's levels are SkinnedMeshes bound to its skeleton); the mesh itself is left as it was. For a BufferGeometry: the same with a new MeshStandardMaterial. For an InstancedMesh: `setLevels` with the simplified geometries and their distances, and the mesh back. A geometry with more than one group is a TypeError (one group, as built-in shapes have, carries over as a group of the whole level). The work is native, charged to the call's fuel in proportion to what it did; a geometry has at most 1,048,576 vertices and triangles (RangeError).

```ts
export function generateLods(target: Mesh | BufferGeometry, options?: GenerateLodsOptions): LOD;
```

## The levels of detail's triangle budget (since API\_MINOR 45)

### LOD\_BUDGET\_MINOR

*const*

```ts
export const LOD_BUDGET_MINOR: number;
```

45 from host API 1.45 (undefined before: feature-detect with `import * as scene from "starhermit:scene"` and `scene.LOD_BUDGET_MINOR !== undefined`): `LodBudget` and `renderer.lodBudget`.

### LodBudgetOptions

*interface*

`new LodBudget(options)`'s options (since API\_MINOR 45).

```ts
export interface LodBudgetOptions { … }
```

- `triangles?: number;`

  The most triangles the members draw a frame: 0 or more, `Infinity` for no limit (default 1,000,000). Every visible instance draws at least its coarsest level, whose triangles count even past it.

- `errorPx?: number;`

  The floor in pixels: no instance refines past a level whose projected error is at most this (finite, 0 or more; default 1).

- `hysteresis?: number;`

  How far, as a fraction, an instance's error must fall below what won it a finer level before it gives the level back (finite, 0 or more; default 0.1).

- `screenHeight?: number | null;`

  The viewport height errors are measured on, in pixels (default null: the renderer's drawing buffer's).

### LodBudget

*class*

ENGINE EXTENSION (since API\_MINOR 45; absent before): a scene-wide triangle budget over levels of detail. Its members are three.js `LOD`s whose levels are meshes and `InstancedMesh`es with levels (`setLevels`), each level's geometry carrying its error in world units as `userData.lodError` (as `generateLods` makes them; level 0's may be left out and counts as 0). A level's triangles are its geometry's index count (or position count) over 3.

While it is `renderer.lodBudget`, each frame (in the scene's sync, once the camera is known, before shadows and drawing) it chooses its members' levels for `renderer.camera` in place of their distances: every visible instance starts at its coarsest level, and the instance whose level shows the largest projected error is refined to its next finer level first, until the next refinement would pass `triangles` or every error is at most `errorPx`. The projected error of a level is `lodError × scale × screenHeight × zoom / (2 tan(fov / 2) × distance)` pixels for a PerspectiveCamera (`scale` the instance's largest world axis scale, `distance` from the camera to its geometry's bounding sphere's center) and `lodError × scale × screenHeight × zoom / (top - bottom)` for an OrthographicCamera; ties go to the member added first, then the lower instance index. Instances out of the camera's frustum (their geometry's bounding sphere, for a `frustumCulled` member) cost nothing and draw their coarsest level (and cast its shadow).

Hysteresis: an instance that drew finer than a level last frame counts that level's error `1 + hysteresis` times, for the floor and for the order, so a refinement is kept until its error falls that fraction below what won it and two instances near the same error do not trade levels frame after frame. With `hysteresis` 0 each frame is chosen afresh.

The choice runs natively (the same Rust in browsers, so the same levels), in O(n log n) for n member instances, its buffers kept from frame to frame; it is charged to the frame's fuel by its instances and refinements. Render-target passes draw the levels the frame chose. A member that is not drawn (invisible or under an invisible parent, not in the scene, not on the camera's layers, or an LOD whose `autoUpdate` is false) is left out and keeps its own levels; so is one whose levels lose their `lodError` after it was added (with a console warning). An LOD in the budget shows its chosen level as `getCurrentLevel()` and its levels' `visible`; its `update(camera)` called by the game is three.js's as ever. Out of a budget, or with `renderer.lodBudget` null, LODs and InstancedMeshes choose by distance as before.

```ts
export class LodBudget { … }
```

- `constructor(options?: LodBudgetOptions);`
- `readonly isLodBudget: true;`

- `triangles: number;`

  See `LodBudgetOptions` (RangeError outside its range).

- `errorPx: number;`
- `hysteresis: number;`
- `screenHeight: number | null;`

- `add(...objects: (LOD | InstancedMesh)[]): this;`

  Adds members (an LOD whose levels are not all meshes with known errors, or anything else, is a TypeError); a member of another budget moves to this one.

- `remove(...objects: (LOD | InstancedMesh)[]): this;`

  Takes members out: they go back to their own levels.

- `has(object: unknown): boolean;`

- `readonly members: readonly (LOD | InstancedMesh)[];`

  The members in the order they were added (a frozen copy).

- `readonly trianglesUsed: number;`

  Last frame's triangles drawn by the members.

- `readonly thresholdPx: number;`

  Last frame's effective threshold: the largest projected error, in pixels, of any drawn instance's level (at most `errorPx` when the floor stopped the refining, above it when the budget did).

- `readonly drawn: number;`

  Last frame's member instances drawn (in view) and culled.

- `readonly culled: number;`

- `readonly refinements: number;`

  Last frame's refinements.

- `readonly limitedBy: "none" | "floor" | "budget";`

  What stopped last frame's refining: `"budget"` (the next refinement would pass `triangles`), `"floor"` (every error within `errorPx`) or `"none"` (every instance at its finest, or no frame yet).

*class*

Points (three.js `Points`): a square per vertex of the geometry's `position` in its draw range, colored by its `color` attribute when the material has `vertexColors`. Each point counts as a mesh instance (a scene draws at most 65,536 points in 1,024 Points objects); points cast no shadows.

export type ParticleVector = { x: number; y: number; z: number } | readonly [number, number, number];
```

### ParticleEmitterOptions

*interface*

A `ParticleEmitter`'s settings (since API\_MINOR 37). Vectors are in the emitter's space: its axes and scale.

```ts
export interface ParticleEmitterOptions { … }
```

- `capacity?: number;`

  The most particles alive at once, 1 to 16,384 (default 256). Fixed when made; a game's emitters hold at most 32,768 together and a game has at most 256 emitters (a RangeError past either).

- `material?: Material;`

  Point sprites: a `PointsMaterial` (default: a new one). Instanced: any mesh material (default: a new `MeshBasicMaterial`).

- `geometry?: BufferGeometry | null;`

  Draws each particle as an instance of this geometry (default null: point sprites).

- `seed?: number;`

  The random stream's seed, an integer 0 to 2^32 − 1 (default 1).

- `rate?: number;`

  Particles a second, spread evenly through each frame (default 0: only bursts).

- `life?: number | readonly [number, number];`

  A particle's life in seconds, or \[min, max\] (uniformly between; 0.001 to 3600; default 1). Since API\_MINOR 40 longer lives too, and `Infinity` (alone or as the longer end): every particle lives until cleared, its ramps held at their first values.

- `space?: "world" | "local";`

  "world" (default): particles spawn where the emitter is and stay in the world as it moves on. "local": they move with it.

- `shape?: "point" | "box" | "sphere" | "shell" | "ring" | "disc";`

  Where particles start round the emitter's origin (or a burst's point): "point" (default), "box" (anywhere within ±`extent` on each axis), "sphere" (anywhere within radius `extent`) or "shell" (on that sphere). Since API\_MINOR 40 also "ring" (on a circle of radius `extent` in the emitter's XZ plane) and "disc" (anywhere within it).

- `extent?: number | ParticleVector;`

  The box's half extents (a number: a cube) or the sphere's radius.

- `velocity?: ParticleVector;`

  A spawned particle's velocity (units a second; default 0), plus up to ±`velocitySpread` on each axis, plus a speed from `speed` along a direction within `spread` radians of `direction` (π: any).

- `velocitySpread?: number | ParticleVector;`

- `speed?: number | readonly [number, number];`

  A number, or \[min, max\] (default 0).

- `direction?: ParticleVector;`

  Default \[0, 1, 0\].

- `spread?: number;`

  0 to π radians (default 0).

- `gravity?: ParticleVector;`

  Acceleration in units a second squared (default 0).

- `drag?: number;`

  Each frame's velocity is divided by 1 + drag × delta (default 0).

- `size?: number | readonly number[];`

  A size factor, or 1 to 8 of them evenly spaced over each life (default 1). Points: times the material's `size` (pixels, or with `sizeAttenuation` world units as three.js's PointsMaterial). Instances: the instance's scale.

- `color?: ColorInput;`

  The particles' color (default white; linear values above 1 bloom): multiplies the material's color.

- `colors?: readonly ColorInput[];`

  1 to 8 colors evenly spaced over each life, in place of `color`.

- `opacity?: number | readonly number[];`

  0 to 1, or 1 to 8 values evenly spaced over each life (default 1): multiplies the material's opacity (a `transparent` material shows it).

- `twinkle?: ParticleTwinkle | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 38 (an unknown option before): each particle's own oscillation, a star's twinkle (default null: none).

- `scale?: number | ParticleVector;`

  Since API\_MINOR 38: instances' scale on each axis, times `size` (default 1; 0 to 4,096). Point sprites leave it out.

- `scaleSpread?: number | ParticleVector;`

  Since API\_MINOR 38: up to ± this much of `scale` on each axis, a factor of each particle's own (default 0; never below 0), so pieces of debris differ in shape.

Since API\_MINOR 40 (PARTICLE\_FORCES\_MINOR; unknown options before). Forces and colliders act in the particles' space: the world's, or the emitter's with `space: "local"`. Wind, curl and the vortex move the air, which carries a particle through its `drag` (without drag they do nothing), as Solstice's particles do. An emitter using any of these steps its particles one at a time (no column layout), still deterministically, natively and in browsers alike.

- `wind?: ParticleVector;`

  The air's velocity (units a second; default 0).

- `curl?: number | ParticleCurl | null;`

  Curl noise moving the air (swirls that neither bunch particles up nor thin them out): a strength (units a second), or \{ strength, scale (feature size, default 4), change (cells a second, default 0.2) \}; null none.

- `buoyancy?: number;`

  Upward acceleration at birth, fading to none at the end of its life (hot gas; default 0).

- `vortex?: number;`

  The air turning about `direction` through the emitter's origin, radians a second (default 0).

- `attract?: number;`

  Acceleration towards the emitter's origin (default 0).

- `floor?: number | (ParticleCollider & { height?: number }) | null;`

  A floor: its height (a +Y plane particles slide along, "clamp"), or a collider with a `height` (default null: none).

- `colliders?: readonly ParticleCollider[] | null;`

  Planes and heightfields, at most 4 with the floor.

- `sway?: number | ParticleSway | null;`

  A wobble drawn about each particle's path (it does not move the particle): an amplitude, or \{ amplitude (a number or per axis; x and y follow a sine, z its cosine, so equal x and z sway in a circle), frequency (cycles a second, or \[min, max\], each particle its own; default 1) \}. Each particle has its own phase, hashed as twinkle's.

- `velocityMode?: "cone" | "planar" | "radial";`

  How `speed` is pointed: "cone" (default: within `spread` of `direction`), "planar" (anywhere in the plane across `direction`: a ring of spray) or "radial" (out from the origin through the spawn point, `direction` at the origin).

- `sizeSpread?: number;`

  Each particle's size times 1 ± this (0 to 1, its own factor).

- `lit?: boolean;`

  Point sprites lit as surfaces are (default false): camera-facing quads `material.size` world units across with a Lambert material made from the PointsMaterial (its color, map, opacity, blending), lit by the sun through its shadow maps with a Henyey–Greenstein phase (`phase`), by the environment and ambient light, and by the scene's other lights as a quad facing the camera. Every light a lit material takes reaches them (up to 16 a frame, each through its own shadow maps where the emitter receives shadows); unlike Solstice's particles, which trace only the two strongest lights at each particle past walls, no light is picked out or traced. GPU emitters' lit particles are lit the same way. ENGINE EXTENSION.

- `soft?: number;`

  Point sprites fading into the scene where they meet it, over this many units of view depth (`renderer.sceneDepth`; default 0: none): camera-facing quads as with `lit`, blended. ENGINE EXTENSION.

- `phase?: number;`

  A lit particle's scattering asymmetry, −1 to 1 (default 0.2: mostly onward, so mist glows with the sun behind it).

- `billboard?: boolean;`

  Point sprites as camera-facing quads `material.size` world units across, unlit (default false; `lit` and `soft` draw so too), as GPU emitters draw theirs. ENGINE EXTENSION.

- `rotation?: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40 (`PARTICLE_ROTATION_MINOR`; an unknown option before): each particle's angle as it spawns, in radians (default 0; −10^6 to 10^6), plus up to ± `rotationSpread` of its own (default 0; π: any angle). With `spin` it turns at `spin` radians a second (the same range; default 0), plus up to ± `spinSpread` of its own (default 0), so confetti flutters each at its own pace: its angle at age a is its start plus its spin × a (no drag, no ramp). Each particle's share of the spreads (and its axis) is hashed from its spawn number and the seed, never drawn from the random stream, so nothing else about the particles changes and live ones turn too. Point sprites (and `lit`, `soft` or `billboard` quads) turn in the view about their centres, counterclockwise on the screen for a positive angle (as three.js's `SpriteMaterial.rotation`), their `map` with them; instances turn about `rotationAxis`.

- `rotationSpread?: number;`
- `spin?: number;`
- `spinSpread?: number;`

- `rotationAxis?: ParticleVector | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40: the axis instances turn about, in the particles' space (made a unit vector; not zero). Default null: each particle an axis of its own, uniform over the sphere, so debris tumbles. Point sprites and their quads ignore it.

### ParticleCollider

*interface*

Since API\_MINOR 40: a plane (the default) or a heightfield particles collide with, in the particles' space.

```ts

- `normal?: ParticleVector;`

- `offset?: number;`

- `heights?: ArrayLike<number>;`

  A heightfield instead: `columns × rows` heights (2 to 256 each way, x fastest, 65,536 at most over an emitter's colliders) over `size` (\[x, z\]) from `origin` (\[x, z\], its least corner), bilinear between them; solid below, nothing outside its area.

- `columns?: number;`
- `rows?: number;`
- `origin?: readonly [number, number];`
- `size?: readonly [number, number];`

- `response?: "bounce" | "clamp" | "stick" | "kill";`

  "bounce" (a collider's default: `restitution` of the speed into the surface comes back out), "clamp" (a floor's default: it slides along), "stick" (it stays there, still ageing) or "kill".

- `restitution?: number;`

  0 to 1 (default 0.5).

- `friction?: number;`

  The share of the speed along the surface lost at each contact, 0 to 1 (default 0).

*interface*

A per-particle oscillation (since API\_MINOR 38). Each particle has a phase and a frequency of its own, hashed from its spawn number and the seed (the random stream is untouched, and live particles twinkle as soon as it is set). Its opacity is multiplied by `1 − opacity × w` and its size by `1 − size × w`, w going 0 → 1 → 0 once a cycle.

## Audio in the scene (three.js r185's audio objects, host API 1.37)

starhermit:audio's graph placed by the scene: an `AudioListener` (on a camera, usually) moves `context.listener`, and each `PositionalAudio` its PannerNode, once a frame after the scene's sync, ramping to where their objects are over the frame's delta as three.js does (a PositionalAudio only while it plays; since API\_MINOR 42, `AUDIO_FOLLOW_SUSPENDED_MINOR`, while the context is suspended they set their parameters at its time instead of ramping, so a held mixer clock never fills the automation queue). They need starhermit:audio imported and `SPATIAL_AUDIO_MINOR` (37): a TypeError otherwise. Buffers are starhermit:audio's `AudioBuffer`s (`context.decodeAudioData`, `createBuffer`); sounds of clips placed in 3D are `play(clip, { position })`, which follow the same listener.

### ParticleEmitter

*class*

Since API\_MINOR 37 (`PARTICLE_EMITTER_MINOR`; constructing one in an older game throws a TypeError): a pool of particles the runtime itself spawns, moves (velocity, gravity, drag), colors, fades and sizes over their lives and draws, once a frame after `onRender` and the scene's sync, so a game pays nothing in script per particle. Add it to the scene as any object; set it up once and change it now and then (`set`, `rate`), and `burst` it. Without a `geometry` its particles are point sprites drawn with its `PointsMaterial`; with one they are instances of it. Seeded and stepped by the frame's delta (the delta `onUpdate` gets, at most 0.25 s a frame), with the engine's own arithmetic, so the same frames give the same particles natively and in browsers: replays and render checks repeat. A step costs the frame's fuel one unit an emitter and one each 8 live particles. Points of all emitters together count toward a frame's 65,536 points, instances toward the instanced meshes' budget.

```ts
export class ParticleEmitter extends Object3D { … }
```

- `constructor(options?: ParticleEmitterOptions);`
- `readonly isParticleEmitter: true;`
- `material: Material;`
- `geometry: BufferGeometry | null;`

- `readonly capacity: number;`

  Fixed when made.

- `seed: number;`

  Changing it starts the random stream again.

- `rate: number;`

  Particles a second.

- `paused: boolean;`

  A paused emitter neither moves nor spawns (its particles still draw).

- `readonly count: number;`

  Its live particles, as of the last frame's step.

- `readonly options: ParticleEmitterOptions;`

  A copy of its settings.

- `set(options: ParticleEmitterOptions): this;`

  Changes some settings (all but `capacity`); the live particles stay and keep their lives. Since API\_MINOR 40 a set the range check refuses (a RangeError) leaves every setting as it was (before, the refused values stayed and the next frame's sync threw).

- `burst(count?: number, at?: ParticleVector, options?: ParticleBurstOptions): this;`

  Spawns `count` particles (default 1) at the next step, at `at` in the emitter's space (default its origin) plus the shape's offset. Past the capacity they are dropped. At most 256 bursts wait for a step: since API\_MINOR 40 one more is a RangeError (before, it was dropped). Since API\_MINOR 43 (`PARTICLE_FLIPBOOK_MINOR`) as many as its capacity wait (each burst spawns at least one particle, so a step's work stays within what the emitter holds; each call is charged as script).

- `prewarm(seconds: number): this;`

  Since API\_MINOR 38 (absent before): runs it `seconds` (0 to 600) ahead now, from where it is, as frames of at most 0.25 s would, paused or not, so a steady emitter starts full. Charged as those steps (one unit each and one each 8 particles), each before it runs. Since API\_MINOR 40 it runs the settings a `set` made this frame (1.38 and 1.39 ran the last frame's until the sync sent them).

- `clear(): this;`

  Lets every live particle go.

- `dispose(): void;`

  Lets its particles and its capacity go; it draws nothing after.

- `radius?: number;`

  The background's corner radius, in font sizes (default 0.25).

- `align?: "left" | "center" | "right";`

  Lines (split at "\\n") aligned within the widest (default "center").

- `lineHeight?: number;`

  Line spacing, in font sizes (default 1.2).

- `anchor?: readonly [number, number] | { x: number; y: number };`

  The label's point at its position: \[0, 0\] its bottom left, \[1, 1\] its top right (default \[0.5, 0.5\]; `center` for a billboard, as Sprite's).

- `resolution?: number;`

  World labels: texture pixels a font size (default 64). Pixel labels are laid out at the window's scale, a texture pixel a window pixel. A label larger than a canvas may be (4096 pixels a side, 2^23 in all) is laid out scaled down to fit, as large but coarser.

- `opacity?: number;`

  The material's opacity (default 1).

### TextLabel

*class*

Text in the scene (since API\_MINOR 37, `TEXT_LABELS_MINOR`; older games' constructor throws a TypeError), for names, scores and tile numerals without a canvas bake in script: the runtime lays the text out with the engine's text stack (shaping, fallback fonts, emoji, as canvas text) into a texture of the label's own in one call, and again only when what it shows changes (its text, font, colors, outline, background, padding, alignment or resolution; not its position, world size, depth test or opacity). Add it to the scene like any object; it draws as a Sprite (`billboard`, the default) or as a plane mesh, with a SpriteMaterial or MeshBasicMaterial whose `map` is its texture (not tone mapped, no fog, transparent, not writing depth).

Like three-spritetext's `SpriteText`, the label sets its own `scale` from its text: size it with `size`. A world label's line is `size` world units of font; a pixel label (`units: "pixels"`) is `size` CSS pixels of font whatever its distance, fitted after `onRender` to the window's camera (`renderer.camera`) and the window's height (in other cameras' views it keeps that scale). It has no raycast. Each label holds a canvas and a texture image (against the game's canvas and image budgets) until `dispose()`, or until it is collected (a label that finds no room in the canvas budget releases dropped ones first). Settings that throw (`set`, the setters) leave it as it was.

```ts
export class TextLabel extends Object3D { … }
```

- `constructor(text?: string, options?: TextLabelOptions);`
- `constructor(options: TextLabelOptions);`
- `readonly isTextLabel: true;`

- `text: string;`

  The text shown; setting the same text again lays nothing out.

- `readonly material: SpriteMaterial | MeshBasicMaterial;`

  What draws it (its own; replaced as `billboard` changes).

- `readonly geometry: BufferGeometry;`

  A fixed label's plane (shared by labels of its anchor).

- `readonly center: Vector2;`

  Its anchor, as Sprite's `center`.

- `readonly options: TextLabelOptions;`

  A copy of its settings.

- `set(options: TextLabelOptions): this;`

  Changes some settings; it lays out again only if what it shows changed.

- `readonly width: number;`

  Its size: world units for a world label, CSS pixels for a pixel label.

- `readonly height: number;`

- `dispose(): void;`

  Lets its texture, canvas and materials go; it draws nothing after.

export type EasingName =
  | "linear"
  | "easeInQuad" | "easeOutQuad" | "easeInOutQuad"
  | "easeInCubic" | "easeOutCubic" | "easeInOutCubic"
  | "easeInQuart" | "easeOutQuart" | "easeInOutQuart"
  | "easeInQuint" | "easeOutQuint" | "easeInOutQuint"
  | "easeInSine" | "easeOutSine" | "easeInOutSine"
  | "easeInExpo" | "easeOutExpo" | "easeInOutExpo"
  | "easeInCirc" | "easeOutCirc" | "easeInOutCirc"
  | "easeInBack" | "easeOutBack" | "easeInOutBack"
  | "easeInElastic" | "easeOutElastic" | "easeInOutElastic"
  | "easeInBounce" | "easeOutBounce" | "easeInOutBounce";
```

Robert Penner's easings as easings.net names them, and `linear` (since API\_MINOR 37).

### TweenOptions

*interface*

A tween's timing and callbacks (since API\_MINOR 37). Times are seconds of the frames' deltas.

```ts
export interface TweenOptions { … }
```

- `duration?: number;`

  Seconds a run takes (default 1; 0 jumps to the end values).

- `delay?: number;`

  Seconds before it starts (default 0).

- `easing?: EasingName;`

  Default `"linear"`.

- `repeat?: number;`

  Runs after the first (default 0; `Infinity` repeats until stopped).

- `yoyo?: boolean;`

  Every other run goes back from the end values to the start values with the same easing (tween.js's yoyo).

- `repeatDelay?: number;`

  Seconds before each repeat, held at the run's end (default 0).

- `from?: Record<string, unknown>;`

  Start values for some of the tweened properties, in the same forms as `to` (default: each property's value when the tween starts).

- `paused?: boolean;`

  Starts paused.

- `onComplete?: () => void;`

  Once it finishes (not when stopped), after its end values were written.

- `onRepeat?: () => void;`

  As each repeat begins.

### tween

*function*

```ts
export function tween(target: object, to: Record<string, unknown>, options?: TweenOptions): Tween;
```

Since API\_MINOR 37 (`TWEENS_MINOR`; older games' calls throw a TypeError): eases `target`'s properties to the values in `to`, stepped by the runtime itself, so no script runs a frame for a tween's timing and easing. A property is

- a number (`material.opacity`, `light.intensity`, a uniform's `value`, any numeric field of a plain object);
- a Vector2, Vector3 or Vector4 (`position`, `scale`): `to` gives a vector, `{ x, y, z }`, `[x, y, z]` or one number for every component;
- a Color (`material.color`, `emissive`): any `ColorLike`, lerped in linear light as `Color.lerp`;
- an Euler (`rotation`): `[x, y, z]` or `{ x, y, z }`, its angles lerped and set with `rotation.set` (its order kept);
- a Quaternion (`quaternion`): a quaternion, `[x, y, z, w]` or an Euler, slerped as three.js r185's `Quaternion.slerp` and set with `quaternion.set`.

So `tween(mesh, { position: [0, 2, 0], scale: 1.5 })`, `tween(mesh.material, { opacity: 0 })` and `tween(material.uniforms.glow, { value: 1 })`.

Timing is tween.js's (three.js's examples' tween library) in seconds: after `delay`, `repeat + 1` runs of `duration`, each repeat after `repeatDelay`; the start values are read as the tween starts (as its delay ends) unless `from` gives them. Once a frame, just before `onUpdate` (and `nextFrame`'s callbacks), every running tween advances by the frame's delta (`frame().delta`) and its values are written as plain assignments (`position.x = …`; Euler and Quaternion through their `set`, so the other follows), so script reads them as it would its own and `onUpdate` may still change them. Then, in the order the tweens were made, repeats call `onRepeat` and finished tweens call `onComplete` and resolve `finished`. Time is summed from the frames' deltas and the easings use the engine's own powers and angles, so the same frames give the same values bit for bit natively and in browsers (replays and render checks repeat).

A tween takes over the properties it drives as it starts: an older tween of the same property of the same object lets that property go, and stops (`finished` false) once it drives none. A property a plain assignment cannot store (read-only, a getter without a setter, a frozen or non-extensible object's, an array's `length`) throws a TypeError here. At most 16,384 tweens at once (RangeError) and 64 properties a tween; a step costs the frame's fuel about one unit a tweened property.

### Tween

*class*

A running tween (since API\_MINOR 37), made by `tween`.

```ts
export class Tween { … }
```

- `private constructor();`

- `readonly target: object;`

  The object `tween` was given.

- `readonly finished: Promise<boolean>;`

  Resolves true when it finishes, false when it is stopped (`stop`, `stopTweens`, or other tweens took all its properties over).

- `readonly running: boolean;`

  Whether it is waiting out its delay or running.

- `paused: boolean;`

  A paused tween keeps its values and its place in time.

- `pause(): this;`
- `resume(): this;`

- `readonly progress: number;`

  Its current run's progress before easing, 0 to 1 (0 while delayed, 1 once it ended).

- `stop(): this;`

  Stops it where it is: `finished` resolves false, no `onComplete`.

- `end(): this;`

  Writes the values its last run ends on (for a tween repeating forever, the end of a forward run) and finishes it at once: `onComplete` runs and `finished` resolves true.

Since API\_MINOR 37: easing `name` at `t` (0 to 1 is the run; the curves go on outside it), the values tweens use.

### Line

*class*

A line through the geometry's `position` vertices (three.js `Line`, since API\_MINOR 17), by its index when it has one, within its draw range, drawn one pixel wide with a `LineBasicMaterial` (another material is a TypeError as the scene syncs). Lines cast no shadows, take no part in ambient occlusion or the scene-depth texture (`renderer.sceneDepth`), are culled by their vertices' bounds, and rays pass through them (three.js's line picking and `raycaster.params.Line` are not supported). A geometry a line draws makes a line mesh, counted against the mesh budget, which lines drawing that geometry alike (the same kind, with or without its colors) share; changing its positions, colors, index or draw range makes it again.

## Cameras

### Camera

*class*

Objects and lights parented to a camera (a held item, a headlamp) draw only once the camera itself is added to the scene, as in three.js.

```ts
export abstract class Camera extends Object3D { … }
```

- `near: number;`
- `far: number;`

- `projectionMatrix: Matrix4;`

  As three.js: from the camera's own aspect or edges. Before API\_MINOR 20 the window's camera (`renderer.camera`) without a view offset takes the window's current aspect, as it draws; every other camera (one kept for maths, such as a probe a view is fitted through, for `project`, `unproject`, `Raycaster.setFromCamera` or a `Frustum`) takes its own on every minor.

  Since API\_MINOR 34 (`CAMERA_PROJECTION_MINOR`) it is the camera's own Matrix4, as three.js's: a game may write its elements (or assign another Matrix4), and the camera then draws with what it holds until `updateProjectionMatrix()` makes it again from the camera's settings. That is three.js's Reflector's oblique near plane (elements 2, 6, 10 and 14 from the mirror plane, so the mirror camera clips exactly at it), or any projection a port builds (`makePerspective`, a jittered or shifted frustum). A written matrix decides the frame's clipping, depth and frustum culling (from its own clip volume, so an oblique near plane culls what lies wholly beyond it), `project`, `unproject` and `Raycaster.setFromCamera`, the background's directions, and the post effects' and ambient occlusion's projection; `near` and `far` stay the camera's (picking rays start at `near`, shadow cascades slice `near` to `far`, and `sceneDepth` and fog measure distance along the view axis, so neither reads the projection). The matrix is three.js's WebGL one (clip depth -1 to 1), mapped to each GPU's own. Unlike three.js, a camera whose matrix was never written follows its settings at once (changing `fov` draws without `updateProjectionMatrix()`, as on older minors). A matrix that is not finite draws with the settings' projection; a singular one draws nothing. Before API\_MINOR 34 it is read-only in effect: it is made from the settings each time it is read, and what a game writes into it is lost.

- `projectionMatrixInverse: Matrix4;`

  The projection's inverse. Since API\_MINOR 34 a game may write it as three.js's Reflector does (`projectionMatrixInverse.copy( projectionMatrix).invert()`); unless written it is the inverse of `projectionMatrix` as it is then (written or made).

- `readonly matrixWorldInverse: Matrix4;`

- `updateProjectionMatrix(): void;`

  three.js's: since API\_MINOR 34 it makes `projectionMatrix` (and its inverse) from the camera's settings again, dropping a written one; before it the projection follows the settings without it.

*interface*

A camera's view offset (three.js `camera.view`, since API\_MINOR 16): what `setViewOffset` sets. Its fields may be changed in place, as in three.js; the scene's sync reads them.

```

- `enabled: boolean;`
- `fullWidth: number;`
- `fullHeight: number;`
- `offsetX: number;`
- `offsetY: number;`

- `height: number;`

### PerspectiveCamera

*class*

Looks down its -Z. `fov` is the vertical field of view in degrees (three.js). From API\_MINOR 20 the projection takes `aspect` as three.js does (a game keeps it at the window's, `engine.frame()`'s width over height, or the image stretches); before it the aspect follows the window. `far` may be Infinity.

```ts
export class PerspectiveCamera extends Camera { … }
```

- `constructor(fov?: number, aspect?: number, near?: number, far?: number);`
- `fov: number;`

- `aspect: number;`

  From API\_MINOR 20 always the projection's, as three.js's. Before it the window's camera (`renderer.camera`) draws with the window's aspect without a view offset, and its `projectionMatrix` follows; with one, or for any other camera's `projectionMatrix`, it is used as three.js uses it (`setViewOffset` sets it to `fullWidth / fullHeight`).

- `view: CameraView | null;`

  three.js's view offset (since API\_MINOR 16): null until `setViewOffset`; `enabled` false after `clearViewOffset`.

- `setViewOffset(fullWidth: number, fullHeight: number, x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number): void;`

  three.js `setViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16): the window shows the `width` × `height` part at `x`, `y` (from the top-left corner, y down) of a `fullWidth` × `fullHeight` image the camera would fill, in any units, and `aspect` becomes `fullWidth / fullHeight`. The projection is then three.js's own, which moves its centre: say, `setViewOffset(w, h, -panel, 0, w + panel, h)` keeps what the camera looks at centred in the window's right `w` beside a `panel` on the left. A size of 0 or a value that is not finite draws nothing, as in three.js. Natively and in browsers alike.

- `clearViewOffset(): void;`

  three.js `clearViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16): the projection is centered on the window's aspect again.

- `updateProjectionMatrix(): void;`

  Kept for ports; projection changes apply without it (since API\_MINOR 34 it also drops a written `projectionMatrix`, as in three.js).

### OrthographicCamera

*class*

From API\_MINOR 20 three.js's projection: `left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom` (asymmetric ones too) and `zoom` as given, whatever the window's aspect (a game keeps `right - left` at the window's aspect times `top - bottom`, or the image stretches, as in three.js; nothing changes them when the window does). Before it the view is centered: `top - bottom` sets its height in world units and the width follows the window's aspect (`left`/`right` are kept but not used for the extent, unless a view offset is set); that is the window's camera's (`renderer.camera`) drawing and `projectionMatrix`, while any other camera's `projectionMatrix` is three.js's on every minor.

```ts
export class OrthographicCamera extends Camera { … }
```

- `constructor(left?: number, right?: number, top?: number, bottom?: number, near?: number, far?: number);`
- `left: number;`
- `right: number;`
- `top: number;`
- `bottom: number;`
- `zoom: number;`

- `view: CameraView | null;`

  three.js's view offset (since API\_MINOR 16), as `PerspectiveCamera.view`.

- `setViewOffset(fullWidth: number, fullHeight: number, x: number, y: number, width: number, height: number): void;`

  three.js `setViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16): while it is set the projection is three.js's from `left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom` and `zoom` (so `right - left` should keep the window's aspect), showing the `width` × `height` part at `x`, `y` of the `fullWidth` × `fullHeight` image they span.

- `clearViewOffset(): void;`

  three.js `clearViewOffset` (since API\_MINOR 16).

- `updateProjectionMatrix(): void;`

## Lights

Intensities (top of file) are three.js r155+'s from API\_MINOR 23, so a port keeps three.js's; before it they are the engine's legacy ones, π times those, and a port from r155+ divides every light's `intensity` here by `Math.PI`. At most 16 lights besides ambient light draw, and four shadow-casting lights: the first four directional or spot lights (in scene order) with `castShadow` cast, each with its own shadow map; other lights' shadows are ignored.

Since API\_MINOR 43 (games declaring `engine.minor=43` or later) point and spot lights are clustered, as Unity URP's Forward+ lights its additional lights: up to 64 a frame besides the 16 light slots (which keep directional, hemisphere and probe lights and point lights whose shadow takes a shadow map), so 80 lights besides ambient light draw (`budgets().lights`). The engine culls them per screen tile (16 × 9 over the view) and depth bin (32 along it): a pixel shades only the lights whose reach (`distance`, and a spot's cone) can touch it, each with exactly the falloff, cone and reflection three.js r185 gives it. A light with no `distance` (0) reaches everywhere and costs every pixel; give lights a `distance` to keep them cheap. Past 64 clustered lights, the rest (in scene order) are left out and counted in `stats().skippedObjects`.

Spot lights' shadows (`castShadow`, `shadow.mapSize` and the rest of `SpotLightShadow`, as in three.js) go to a shadow atlas, as URP's additional-lights shadow atlas: up to 8 spots a frame, each map 64 to 1024 texels a side (`mapSize` clamped), side by side in one of the four shadow maps (a grid of cells as wide as the largest map: 1, 2×2 or 3×3). The atlas takes the map after the directional lights' (with three cascades, the fourth); point lights' maps come after it. When more spots cast than fit, 8 win: those whose reach (the cone's range) meets the camera's view, then the nearest the camera, then scene order; the others light unshadowed. `shadow.autoUpdate` false and `needsUpdate` work as in three.js: a kept spot keeps the view its map was drawn with until `needsUpdate`, and while every spot in the atlas is kept and nothing changed the whole atlas is kept (not drawn). When any spot draws (autoUpdate true, needsUpdate, a spot joining or leaving the atlas, or one moving to another cell), the whole atlas is drawn again, each kept spot from its kept view: the same map as three.js keeps unless that spot's casters moved meanwhile (three.js would still show them where they were). Lookups are three.js's PCF or basic (`receiverPlane` takes PCF). Older games' spot lights take one of the four maps each, as before.

```

- `color: Color;`
- `intensity: number;`

### AmbientLight

*class*

Adds color × intensity of irradiance to every lit surface (ambient lights add up): from API\_MINOR 23 through three.js's `BRDF_Lambert`, `base × (1 − metalness) / π` of it, as three.js r155+; before, the legacy units' color × intensity × the whole base color.

```ts
export class AmbientLight extends Light { … }
```

- `constructor(color?: ColorInput, intensity?: number);`

### LightShadow

*interface*

Shadow settings of a casting light.

Since API\_MINOR 23 (games declaring `engine.minor=23` or later) they are three.js r185's `LightShadow`: the map sees what `camera` sees from the light's world position looking at its target's (up +Y), as three.js's `updateMatrices`. A directional light's camera is an `OrthographicCamera(-5, 5, 5, -5, 0.5, 500)`: shadows reach only what its box holds (outside it all is lit), and the box's width over `mapSize` is a texel's size, so the bias a scene needs is the one it needs in three.js. A spot's is a `PerspectiveCamera` whose `fov` is twice the light's `angle` times `focus` (degrees), its aspect `aspect` and its far plane the light's `distance` (or the camera's own `far`, default 500, without one), near 0.5. Set the camera's planes, edges and `zoom` and call its `updateProjectionMatrix()` as in three.js; the shadow follows them each frame. Shadows filter as `renderer.shadowMap.type` says (`PCFShadowMap`: five lookups on a Vogel disk `radius` texels wide, turned per pixel by interleaved gradient noise; `BasicShadowMap`: one nearest texel). Maps draw each material's `shadowSide` (by default the side opposite its `side`), clipped at the camera's near and far planes, a masked material cut out by its map's alpha alone (`alphaTest` against `map`, as three.js's `MeshDepthMaterial`; not `opacity` or vertex colors).

Before API\_MINOR 23 they are the engine's own: a directional light's map is fitted to the camera's view out to `distance`, `bias` acts only when negative and `normalBias` is in map texels (the members marked "before API\_MINOR 23"); the camera's `near` and `far` are `near` and `distance`, and three.js's members below are ignored.

Since API\_MINOR 33 a light may take the engine's receiver-plane filter in place of three.js's (`receiverPlane`, not three.js).

Before API\_MINOR 40 point lights cast no shadows. Since API\_MINOR 40 a point light's `shadow` is three.js r185's `PointLightShadow` (see `PointLight.shadow`). At most four maps are drawn: the directional and spot lights' with `castShadow` in scene order (each cascade a map), then point lights', so point lights lose theirs first, to the slots and to the effect budget (with a note in Options).

```ts
export interface LightShadow { … }
```

- `camera: OrthographicCamera | PerspectiveCamera;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23 the shadow camera (an `OrthographicCamera`, or a spot's `PerspectiveCamera`), which three.js's `copy` clones.

- `mapSize: Vector2 | number;`

  The map's size, 64–4096: a three.js vector (its larger side when not square) or a number. Since API\_MINOR 23 the default is 512 × 512 and the game's size is kept whatever the graphics level (sizes past 4096, or past the device's largest texture, draw at the smaller; each map takes size² × 4 bytes of the GPU's effect budget, and one that does not fit is left out, its light unshadowed, with a note in Options). Before it the default is 2048, and since API\_MINOR 14 the graphics level holds it to its `shadowMapSize` (512 at quantum, 1024 atomic and molecular, 2048 cellular and terrestrial, 4096 above).

- `bias: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23 added to the depth each point is compared at, in the map's 0–1 depth (default 0): negative values move it toward the light, against acne, positive ones away, as three.js's. Before it three.js's sign with only negative values acting (default −0.0005).

- `normalBias: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23 how far each point moves along its vertex normal (turned for back-sided materials) before its lookup, in world units (default 0), as three.js's. Before it a normal offset in map texels (default 1.5).

- `radius: number;`

  The filter's radius in map texels, 0–16 (since API\_MINOR 9; three.js `shadow.radius`, default 1; 0 a hard edge): since API\_MINOR 23 the disk `PCFShadowMap`'s five lookups spread over, before it the spacing of the engine's nine. Outside 0–16 the light's sync throws.

- `intensity: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23: how much the shadow darkens, 0–1 (default 1).

- `focus: number;`

  Spot: the part of the cone the map covers, 0 &lt; focus ≤ 1 (three.js `shadow.focus`, default 1).

- `aspect: number;`

  Spot, since API\_MINOR 23: the camera's aspect (default 1).

- `blurSamples: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23, three.js's (default 8): `VSMShadowMap`'s blur, which the engine does not draw (VSM draws as PCF).

- `autoUpdate: boolean;`

  Since API\_MINOR 23, three.js's (default true and false). Since API\_MINOR 40 they act as three.js r185's: with `autoUpdate` false the map is drawn once and then kept, with the camera it was drawn with (the light may move; its map and lookup do not follow), until `needsUpdate` is set true, which draws it again that frame and goes back to false (`renderer.shadowMap.autoUpdate` and `needsUpdate` do the same for every map). Before API\_MINOR 40 the engine draws every map each frame whatever they say.

- `needsUpdate: boolean;`

- `distance: number;`

  Before API\_MINOR 23: a directional light's reach along the view (default 40 m), a spot's far plane.

- `near: number;`

  Before API\_MINOR 23: a spot's near plane (default 0.5 m).

- ```ts
  cascades?: {
      count?: number;
      maxDistance: number;
      splitLambda?: number;
      /** ENGINE EXTENSION (since API_MINOR 40, after Solstice's cached
       * shadows; default false): the cascades keep their static casters.
       * Casters that have not moved for 30 frames (and are neither skinned
       * nor drawn through a custom material's code) are drawn once into a
       * cache image per cascade, which is copied into the map each frame
       * with the casters that move drawn over it; a cascade draws its
       * cache again only when its view moves a coarse step (a 32nd of its
       * padded width, in whole texels) or out of its padded depth range,
       * when the light turns past its lag (0.03° for the nearest cascade
       * to 0.37° for the farthest), or when a caster joins or leaves the
       * cached ones (starts or
       * stops moving, appears or goes). Since API_MINOR 41 a cached
       * caster also leaves them for 30 frames when what it draws with
       * changes though it stands still (its geometry or draw range, its
       * opacity, its material's alpha, sides or map, that map's pixels
       * written in place, an InstancedMesh's instances updated), a caster
       * whose map is a render target's stays live, and a cascade draws
       * its cache again when its light or the cascades' bounds change;
       * before it only a caster's place counts. Far cascades take turns: at most
       * one draws its cache again a frame. Each cache takes another map's
       * bytes of the effect budget; one that does not fit draws every
       * caster each frame, as without it. Not a boolean is a TypeError;
       * before API_MINOR 40 it is not read. */
      cached?: boolean;
    } | null;
  ```

  ENGINE EXTENSION, not three.js (since API\_MINOR 26; three.js's cascaded shadows are its `three/addons/csm` addon): a directional light's cascaded shadow maps, null (the default) for the one map of its `camera`'s box. With cascades the camera's box and planes are not used: `count` maps (1–4, default 3; each `mapSize`, together within the four maps a pass takes, so other casting lights may lose theirs) split the camera's view from its near plane to `maxDistance` (along the view; its far plane if nearer) as the CSM addon's practical split does, `splitLambda` (0–1, default 0.5, the addon's) blending its even split (0) with its logarithmic one (1). Each map is fitted to its slice, finest nearest, and a point takes the first map holding it. Past the last map (its square box covers the view to `maxDistance` and somewhat beyond, more so for wide views) the light is unshadowed, and casters out of a map's reach are not drawn into it: the cheap way to shadow a large world. `bias`, `normalBias`, `radius`, `intensity` and `renderer.shadowMap.type` apply to every map. Other values are a RangeError, and setting it before API\_MINOR 26 a TypeError, as the scene syncs; spot lights ignore it.

- `receiverPlane?: boolean;`

  ENGINE EXTENSION, not three.js (since API\_MINOR 33; three.js r185 has no receiver-plane bias): a directional or spot light's receiver-plane filter, false (the default) for the filter `renderer.shadowMap.type` gives (three.js's, which shadows a sloped surface at a near-zero `bias`). With true the map is filtered over nine lookups on a square grid `radius` texels apart (one at radius 0), each blending the four texels around it as a linear filter does but comparing each texel at the receiver's plane extended to that texel's centre (its slope from the screen derivatives of the world position), less half a texel's change of that plane on each axis; taps and texels past the map's edge are lit, as is all outside the shadow camera's volume. A sloped surface no longer shadows itself while a true occluder still shadows it fully, so `bias` need only cover depth precision and curvature. `bias`, `normalBias`, `intensity` and cascades apply as before; `renderer.shadowMap.type` does not. It costs 36 depth comparisons a lookup (4 at radius 0; three.js's PCF: five filtered). Other values are a TypeError, as is setting it true before API\_MINOR 33, as the scene syncs. See spec rendering-and-quality.html#receiver-plane.

### PointLight

*class*

`distance` is where its light ends (0: no limit); falls off with the distance to the power `decay` (2, the inverse square, as glTF).

```ts

```

- `constructor(color?: ColorInput, intensity?: number, distance?: number, decay?: number);`
- `distance: number;`
- `decay: number;`

- `readonly shadow: LightShadow;`

  Since API\_MINOR 40, three.js r185's `PointLightShadow` (undefined before): a `PerspectiveCamera(90, 1, 0.5, 500)` per cube face (its far the light's `distance` when set), `mapSize` each face's side (default 512; the map holds the six faces, 3 × `mapSize` square, so at most 1365 a face), `bias` in the face's 0–1 depth, `normalBias` in world units, `radius`, `intensity`, `autoUpdate` and `needsUpdate` as `LightShadow`'s; `PCFShadowMap` filters five lookups on a disk across the direction, `BasicShadowMap` compares the nearest texel, and points nearer than `near` or past `far` are lit, as three.js's `getPointShadow`. The engine has no cube textures: the six faces lie side by side in one 2D depth map.

A cone toward `target`: `angle` (radians, at most π/2) is its edge and `penumbra` (0–1) the fraction of it that fades out. Point lights cast no shadows; spot lights can.

Sky color from above blending to the ground color from below, by the surface normal, as irradiance: from API\_MINOR 23 through three.js's `BRDF_Lambert` of the diffuse color, `base × (1 − metalness) / π`, as three.js r155+; before, times the whole base color (legacy units).

### SphericalHarmonics3

*class*

L2 spherical harmonics (bands 0 to 2) of RGB light, three.js r185's: `coefficients[i]` holds basis function i's red, green and blue (x, y, z), in three.js's order and normalization (the basis is `getBasisAt`'s: 0.282095; 0.488603 × y, z, x; 1.092548 × xy, yz; 0.315392 × (3z² − 1); 1.092548 × xz; 0.546274 × (x² − y²)).

```ts
export class SphericalHarmonics3 { … }
```

- `constructor();`
- `readonly isSphericalHarmonics3: true;`

- `coefficients: Vector3[];`

  Nine coefficients.

- `set(coefficients: Vector3[]): this;`
- `zero(): this;`

- `getAt(normal: Vector3, target: Vector3): Vector3;`

  The radiance in the direction of the unit `normal`, into `target`.

- `getIrradianceAt(normal: Vector3, target: Vector3): Vector3;`

  The irradiance in the direction of the unit `normal` (the radiance convolved with the cosine lobe: 0.886227, 1.023328, 0.858086, 0.743125 z² − 0.247708 and 0.429043 times the bands' terms), into `target`: what a `LightProbe` of intensity 1 lights a surface facing `normal` with.

- `add(sh: SphericalHarmonics3): this;`
- `addScaledSH(sh: SphericalHarmonics3, s: number): this;`
- `scale(s: number): this;`
- `lerp(sh: SphericalHarmonics3, alpha: number): this;`
- `equals(sh: SphericalHarmonics3): boolean;`
- `copy(sh: SphericalHarmonics3): this;`
- `clone(): SphericalHarmonics3;`

- `fromArray(array: ArrayLike<number>, offset?: number): this;`

  The coefficients from 27 numbers (each one's r, g, b in turn) at `offset`.

- `toArray<T extends { [index: number]: number } = number[]>(array?: T, offset?: number): T;`

- `static getBasisAt(normal: Vector3, shBasis: number[]): void;`

  The nine basis functions at the unit `normal`, into `shBasis`.

### LightProbe

*class*

Irradiance from spherical harmonics, three.js r185's `LightProbe`: the scene's probes add up (each coefficient times its probe's `intensity`; `color` is unused, the position and rotation too) and every lit material (standard, physical, Lambert, Phong, toon, and custom materials' `light` hooks as indirect light) takes `sh.getIrradianceAt(normal) × intensity` along its world normal (the shading normal, normal maps included) per pixel as indirect diffuse light, as ambient light: through `BRDF_Lambert` of the diffuse color, ambient occlusion applied. The coefficients are linear light, any sign, within ±65,504 (others throw when the scene syncs). A scene's probes take two of its 16 extra light slots; a custom material that reads the frame's lights itself sees them as kinds 4 and 5. `LightProbeGenerator` is not offered.

```ts
export class LightProbe extends Light { … }
```

- `constructor(sh?: SphericalHarmonics3, intensity?: number);`
- `readonly isLightProbe: true;`
- `sh: SphericalHarmonics3;`

- `toJSON(meta?: unknown): { metadata?: { version: number; type: string; generator: string }; object: Record<string, unknown> };`

  three.js's JSON of the probe (Object3D's fields without children, `color`, `intensity` and `sh`, the coefficients' 27 numbers); its `type` is `"Light"`, as three.js r185 writes it.

### Scene

*class*

The scene the runtime draws (there is one: `scene`).

```ts
export class Scene extends Object3D { … }
```

- `#private;`
- `private constructor();`

- `background: Color | Texture | null;`

  What is behind everything (three.js), in the window and in `renderer.render(scene, camera)` passes into a render target (which once took only `renderer.setClearColor`): a Color clears to it (a pass of the scene clears to it whatever `autoClear` says, as three.js's does), never tone mapped; before API\_MINOR 20 the window's was tone mapped with the scene when post effects or multisampling drew it (from API\_MINOR 20 only when a `renderer.post` program reads the scene); null keeps black (a pass the renderer's clear color). Since API\_MINOR 18 a texture too, drawn over the clear behind everything, unfogged, tone mapped unless its `colorSpace` is `SRGBColorSpace` (three.js r16x's `WebGLBackground`):

  - a Texture or CanvasTexture of `UVMapping` (the default) stretched over the view, its UVs from the view's bottom left as a plane's through its `offset`, `repeat`, `rotation` and `center` (three.js leaves the aspect to them: `repeat.x = viewAspect / imageAspect` and `offset.x = (1 - repeat.x) / 2` cover a wider view);
  - a sky in every direction: a CubeTexture (its images at full detail: package paths load through `TextureLoader` once, counted against the image budget like any texture; nothing shows until all six have; one that cannot load shows the environment instead), a texture whose `mapping` is `EquirectangularReflectionMapping` (or `EquirectangularRefractionMapping`), or a PMREM texture (`PMREMGenerator`'s, which shows its prefiltered 512 × 256 image). `backgroundBlurriness` above 0 shows the sky's prefiltered environment at that roughness (made as `scene.environment` makes one, and shared with it for the same texture: it shows a few frames later); a `FloatType` DataTexture's light past 1 comes from it too. Other values draw nothing.

- `backgroundBlurriness: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 18: a sky background's blur, 0 (sharp, the default) to 1 (three.js `backgroundBlurriness`; clamped).

- `backgroundIntensity: number;`

  Since API\_MINOR 18: a texture or sky background's light is its image's times this (three.js `backgroundIntensity`; default 1).

- `readonly backgroundRotation: Euler;`

  Since API\_MINOR 18: turns a sky background (three.js `backgroundRotation`, as `environmentRotation` turns the environment).

- `fog: Fog | FogExp2 | null;`

- `environment: Texture | null;`

  Lights standard, physical and Lambert (since API\_MINOR 29 also Phong) materials without an `envMap` (three.js): a PMREM texture, a latitude-longitude texture or a CubeTexture (made into a prefiltered environment once per texture version; one that cannot be lights nothing, with a warning).

- `environmentIntensity: number;`

  Default 1.

- `readonly environmentRotation: Euler;`

  Turns the environment (three.js `environmentRotation`).

- `overrideMaterial: Material | null;`

  Since API\_MINOR 35 (`OVERRIDE_MATERIAL_MINOR`; absent before): three.js r185's `overrideMaterial` (default null). While set, every pass of the scene (`renderer.render(scene, camera)` into a target, and the window's frame) draws each object with it in its own material's place: each keeps its geometry (and draw range, groups and morphs), placement, skin, instances, instance colors and shadow flags, and an object its own material hides stays hidden, as in three.js. A pass of an object under the scene ignores it, as three.js's does. Its kind decides what it takes: a `PointsMaterial` the points, a `LineBasicMaterial` the lines, a `wireframe` material the wireframes, any other material the triangle meshes (what an object draws is its own material's geometry here: one that draws lines, points or a wireframe keeps its own material under an override of another kind); sprites keep their own. Set it, render into a target, set it back to null: a depth or ID pass, a shadow map of the game's own.
